questions.stem: A client recovering from a myocardial infarction has chronic constipation and reports needing to strain during bowel movements. Which teaching is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Limit fiber and fluids so bowel movements occur less often, reducing the number of times cardiovascular stress can occur during defecation.","B":"Use the prescribed bowel regimen and avoid straining or prolonged Valsalva-like effort because it can produce marked hemodynamic changes during defecation.","C":"Stop all stool-softening therapy once bowel movements become less frequent because constipation is preferable to medication use after myocardial infarction.","D":"Use repeated forceful bearing down to shorten each bowel movement because brief high-pressure straining places less stress on the circulation."}}
questions.rationale: Straining during defecation produces Valsalva-like hemodynamic changes and can provoke substantial blood-pressure and heart-rate shifts. In a client with cardiovascular disease, preventing constipation and minimizing forceful straining is safer than repeated bearing down.
questions.source_name: PubMed — Constipation-induced pressor effects as triggers for cardiovascular events
questions.source_detail: Review evidence describes straining at stool as a Valsalva-like maneuver that can raise blood pressure and trigger cardiovascular events in susceptible patients.

questions.stem: A client has a heavily exudative sacral wound with repeated strike-through drainage and early periwound maceration. Which dressing strategy best addresses the immediate wound-management problem?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Select an absorptive dressing appropriate for heavy exudate and protect the periwound skin while reassessing drainage and wound characteristics.","B":"Use a transparent film as the primary dressing because occlusion is preferred even when drainage repeatedly saturates the existing dressing.","C":"Leave the wound uncovered so drainage can evaporate, relying on linen changes rather than an absorptive dressing to control the excess moisture.","D":"Continue dry gauze on a fixed schedule regardless of saturation because changing the dressing based on exudate unnecessarily disrupts wound healing."}}
questions.rationale: Heavy exudate requires a dressing that can absorb and retain drainage while protecting the surrounding skin from maceration. Dressing selection should be driven by wound characteristics, including exudate amount, rather than by a fixed schedule or an occlusive film poorly suited to heavy drainage.
questions.source_name: Wound, Ostomy and Continence Nurses Society — Wound management resources
questions.source_detail: Current wound-care principles emphasize matching dressing properties to wound characteristics and managing excess exudate to protect periwound skin.

questions.stem: An older adult with delirium from a urinary infection repeatedly tries to climb out of bed. Which nursing action is most appropriate before considering a physical restraint?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer a sedating medication primarily to keep the client in bed, because chemical restraint is less restrictive than a physical device.","B":"Raise all side rails and leave the client alone in a dark room so environmental stimulation cannot contribute to further attempts to get up.","C":"Apply a waist restraint while the family is present, then evaluate reversible causes after the immediate fall risk has been controlled.","D":"Increase observation, address reversible causes, use environmental safety measures, and try less-restrictive interventions before restraint."}}
questions.rationale: CMS patient-rights requirements prohibit restraint for staff convenience and require restraint use to be limited to situations in which it is necessary for safety. Delirium care should first address reversible causes and use less-restrictive safety strategies when feasible.
questions.source_name: CMS — Hospital Conditions of Participation: Patient Rights, Restraint and Seclusion
questions.source_detail: CMS requires freedom from inappropriate restraint and emphasizes regulated use only when clinically necessary rather than for convenience.

questions.stem: An older adult who uses a hearing aid reports intermittent feedback and reduced amplification. Which nursing action is most appropriate before assuming the device has failed?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Increase the volume to the maximum setting and leave it there because louder amplification is the safest first response to reduced hearing.","B":"Rinse the hearing aid under running water and return it to the ear while still damp because moisture improves sound conduction.","C":"Check that the device is clean, dry, powered, and positioned correctly, and arrange further evaluation if function remains poor.","D":"Store the hearing aid in a warm humid location between uses because moisture prevents the internal components from drying out."}}
questions.rationale: NIDCD recommends keeping hearing aids away from heat and moisture, cleaning them as instructed, turning them off when not in use, and replacing dead batteries. Basic troubleshooting should address these factors before assuming permanent device failure.
questions.source_detail: NIDCD maintenance guidance: keep hearing aids away from heat/moisture, clean as instructed, turn off when not in use, and replace dead batteries.

questions.stem: A postmenopausal client with low bone mass asks which lifestyle plan best supports bone health while the provider completes a fracture-risk assessment. Which response is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid weight-bearing activity because repetitive loading accelerates bone loss once bone mineral density has already begun to decline.","B":"Use adequate calcium and vitamin D intake with appropriate weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening activity tailored to fracture risk.","C":"Increase caffeine intake and avoid resistance exercise because stimulants and rest provide the strongest protection against fragility fractures.","D":"Rely on vitamin supplements alone because exercise, balance training, and fall-risk reduction do not materially affect fracture prevention."}}
questions.rationale: Bone-health guidance supports adequate calcium and vitamin D together with weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise. Exercise selection should reflect the client's fracture risk and physical limitations rather than applying a one-size-fits-all high-impact program.
questions.source_name: Bone Health & Osteoporosis Foundation — Weight-Bearing and Muscle-Strengthening Exercise
questions.source_detail: BHOF identifies weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise as important for building and maintaining bone density.
